clue.text: Detestable group one demonstrating perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: a slang term for a contemptible bunch of people
second meaning: one who shows something

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a crowd of protesters as a loathsome lot.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a whimsical coinage: a person who shows things off, pronounced to rhyme with 'grower', not the bathroom fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses the word for a worthless bunch, while literally it names anyone who displays or exhibits something.

clue.text: In duck way to produce quack?

blocks.note: being in means being at home
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A duck's way of producing its quack.
explanation.walkthrough: Duck and quack set up a farmyard picture; quack here is a disparaging word for an unqualified healer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sceptics call practitioners of unproven remedies quacks, and a homeopath is one example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Old forum was surprisingly well-known

indicators.note: the result of rearranging comes out unexpectedly, in a surprising new order

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman forum turned out to be unexpectedly renowned.
explanation.definitionFit: Being famous across the world is an emphatic way of being widely known.

clue.text: Amber perhaps concerned with lapse

explanation.surface: Something amber-coloured is linked to a slip-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amber' suggests a traffic light colour; it is fossilised tree gum.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is fossilised tree resin, so it is one example of the substance.

clue.text: Occasionally, song bird crossing river makes flaky descent

indicators.note: something done only occasionally happens every other time, so only alternate letters of the next word count
the bird stretches across the river, holding it within its own letters

blocks.note: first and third letters of song
the Fal is a river in Cornwall

explanation.surface: A bird sings over a river as something drifts down from the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fal runs through Cornwall in south-west England; it slips between the second and third letters of the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow comes down in flakes, so a fall of snow is a descent made of flakes.

clue.text: One bounding area between two American cities

indicators.note: something placed between two others ends up sitting inside the pair

blocks.note: New York and Los Angeles, by their usual abbreviations

explanation.surface: Something marking the edge of a zone lying between two US cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One bounding' looks like a boundary; it is an animal that leaps. 'Between two American cities' puts the area letter between two city abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: The nyala is an African antelope, and antelopes are animals that leap and spring along.

clue.text: Was drinking bitter, essentially more than one unit

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only the central letters are kept
something drinking takes another thing inside it

blocks.note: the two central letters of bitter

explanation.surface: Someone was downing a pint of bitter, more than one in fact.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British style of beer, which makes 'drinking' read naturally.
explanation.definitionFit: The watt is the SI unit of power, so the plural is more than one such unit.

clue.text: Almost over — over from the word go

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Something is nearly finished, done from the very start.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'over' is used in two different senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'from the egg', i.e. from the very beginning.

clue.text: Adult daughter, in character, shaking rear — lively sort!

indicators.note: shaking off its rear means the final letter is lost
the two abbreviations are placed in the other word

blocks.note: a letter is a character of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A grown-up daughter dances in character, wiggling her bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaking rear' paints a dancer but means drop the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladette is a British term for a boisterous young woman who behaves in a loud, lads-like way.

clue.text: SMS with cunning content is painful

indicators.note: a thing's content is what is held inside it

blocks.note: taken as written; the cunning goes between the M and the final S

explanation.surface: A sly text message stings its recipient.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'content' tells you the cunning sits inside the three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To smart is to sting or hurt, so something that smarts is causing pain.

clue.text: So daft of Batty to provide rations for the fleet?

indicators.note: batty means crazy, so the preceding words go wild and come out jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a dim-witted cook supplying meals to the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' is not ships here but people who are quick: those on the move eat food that is fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet means swift, and quick takeaway meals suit people in a hurry, a pun on navy rations.

clue.text: Before entrance, Liberal on and on about Democrat's old authority

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the pair of ons wrap around the party member

blocks.note: to entrance is to enrapture, a sense shared by this verb

explanation.surface: A Liberal keeps droning on about a Democrat before an entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before entrance' places the enrapture verb after the rest. 'Entrance' must be read as the verb (en-TRANCE), not a doorway. The authority ran the capital's buses and Tube from 1933 to 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: This body was the public authority running the capital's buses and Underground until replaced by TfL in 2000.

clue.text: Dish very dry steeped in port?

indicators.note: something steeped in liquid sits inside it

blocks.note: Rio de Janeiro is a port

explanation.surface: A dish that's quite dry is soaked in port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' tempts as the fortified wine; it is a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Risotto is an Italian rice dish.

clue.text: Loop ring through snout

indicators.note: the ring passes through the middle of the other word, ending up inside it

explanation.surface: A loop like a bull's ring passed through its nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A noose is a loop of rope with a running knot.

clue.text: Excellent anaesthetic for two or three?

explanation.surface: Someone praises a fine anaesthetic for a couple of patients.
explanation.walkthrough: The second piece is read as numb-er, not a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Two and three are each divisible only by one and themselves, so they are examples of such integers.

clue.text: Five hundred gather with copper entering capital

indicators.note: the metal goes inside, entering the word for gathering

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Five hundred people assemble with a policeman marching into the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a police officer but here is the element's symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the capital city of Syria, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Lift of weight to shoulders — not using steroids?

blocks.note: first meaning: the weightlifting move bringing the bar to shoulder height

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses come from sport, so the clue reads as one weightlifting scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In weightlifting the first phase of the clean and jerk is named thus, and a drug-free athlete is said to be the same word.

clue.text: Sloth's middle toe is damaged and redundant

indicators.note: only the central letter of the animal's name is kept
damaged words are broken and put back together in a new order

blocks.note: the middle letter of the five-letter word sloth

explanation.surface: A sloth has injured a toe, now useless.
explanation.definitionFit: Otiose describes something serving no practical purpose, which is what redundant means.

clue.text: Metal drummers employed in such an ensemble?

definitions.text: Metal drummers employed in such an ensemble?

blocks.note: surface reading: drummers from a heavy-metal rock group
setter's reading: a Caribbean group whose percussionists play pans made of metal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal drummers' suggests heavy-metal rock; the drummers literally play metal instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: This Trinidadian ensemble plays tuned drums hammered from oil barrels.

clue.text: Brilliant finish in church attracted to Catholicism?

blocks.note: Rome stands for the Roman Catholic Church

explanation.surface: A convert drawn to Catholicism admires a church's dazzling decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attracted to' just places the church abbreviation next to the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Chromium plating gives a shiny, mirror-like surface coating to metal objects.

clue.text: My delicate decorative feature

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
nice in the sense of fine or subtle

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a dainty ornamental detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A cornice is an ornamental moulding running along the top of a wall or building.

clue.text: French head drinking English wine looked wobbly

indicators.note: something drinking takes another thing inside it

explanation.surface: A Frenchman who has sunk English wine is unsteady on his feet.
explanation.definitionFit: To teeter is to sway unsteadily, so something that teetered looked wobbly.

clue.text: Is this suggesting brother has a problem?

blocks.clueFragment: Is this suggesting brother has a problem?
blocks.note: surface reading: a sibling has got himself into difficulty
setter's reading: read the phrase as an instruction — the cricket abbreviation for runs goes into a word for trouble, and the result is brother

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a remark hints that a sibling is in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: R for runs placed into BOTHER, a synonym of trouble, gives BROTHER. The answer phrase also plainly means meets difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: To run into trouble is an idiom for encountering difficulties, which is having a problem.

clue.text: Wanderer takes no notice, raking in million

indicators.note: raking in money means gathering it inside

explanation.surface: A wanderer ignores warnings while earning a million.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes no notice' looks like a phrase meaning ignores, but splits into a link word and two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad roams without a fixed home.

clue.text: Bury Football Club appearing at San Siro?

definitions.text: Football Club appearing at San Siro?

blocks.note: first meaning: to place in a grave

blocks.clueFragment: Football Club appearing at San Siro?
blocks.note: second meaning: the Milan club that plays at the San Siro stadium

explanation.walkthrough: Bury is also an English football club, so 'Bury Football Club' reads as one name.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter means to lay in a grave, and Inter Milan shares the San Siro ground with AC Milan.

clue.text: Bored with banks, an executive finally making exit

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the preceding word is wanted
something making its exit leaves, so it is taken out

explanation.surface: An executive leaves the bank, finally fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' suggests finance; here it means rows or levels.
explanation.definitionFit: Tired of something means bored with it.

clue.text: King due favour had words

blocks.note: R for rex, Latin for king
if a favour is due to you, you are owed it

explanation.surface: A king, owed a favour, argued about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer rhymes with 'cowed': to row is a British word for quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Having words with someone is an idiom for arguing, which is what quarrelled means.

clue.text: Green wall up, having bit of a kip inside?

indicators.note: the small coin is put inside the verb for walling up

blocks.note: to immure is to enclose within walls
the kip is the currency of Laos and the at is a hundredth of it

explanation.surface: Someone walls up a sleeping spot, wanting a short nap inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kip' looks like British slang for a nap; it is the Laotian currency, whose small unit is the at.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means inexperienced or not yet grown up, the same as immature.

clue.text: Zoom lens in trap set by river?

blocks.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge

explanation.surface: A photographer zooms in on a snare laid beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zoom lens' suggests a photographer's kit, but Zoom is the video-call service.
explanation.definitionFit: On a Zoom video call, a computer's built-in camera serves as the lens showing your face.

clue.text: Criminal drooled over a fabulously rich city

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: A crook salivated over a city of fabulous wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' simply joins the two parts of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary golden city sought by Spanish conquistadors was fabled for its riches.

clue.text: Laugh at the German plan that's incomplete

indicators.note: an incomplete word is missing its final letter

blocks.note: der is a German word for the

explanation.surface: People mock a German's half-finished scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride someone is to mock or ridicule them, i.e. laugh at them.
